title: Bone Conduction Headphones in 2026: The Best Picks for Runners, Swimmers, and Everyday Adventures
summary: Remember the first time you tried bone conduction headphones? If you’re picturing a ticklish, buzzy mess with tinny sound, you’re stuck in the past. The technology has come a long way, and in 2026, these open-ear wonders are some of the best workout companions you can buy. WIRED’s audio experts put the latest models to the test, and the results might surprise you. Shokz remains the leader, and the OpenSwim Pro is a standout. It fixes the biggest flaw of its predecessor by adding Bluetooth streaming alongside a built-in 32-GB music player—that’s room for about 8,000 songs. With an IP68 waterproof rating, it can handle laps in the pool or a sweaty run, and the sound is surprisingly warm, with solid bass and clear vocals. There’s even an EQ mode specifically for swimming. For runners, the OpenRun Pro 2 is Shokz’s flagship. It combines a bone conduction driver for precise mids and highs with an air conduction speaker for deeper bass, creating a richer sound than ever before. At just 1.1 ounces, you’ll forget you’re wearing it, and the smaller size option is a game-changer for those with smaller heads. Plus, it finally uses USB-C charging. If you’re on a budget, the Nank Runner Diver2 Pro is a rugged alternative. It boasts an IP69 rating—meaning it can survive submerged up to 10 meters deep for five hours—and delivers powerful bass, though you might need to fiddle with the fit to get the best sound. For those who want a premium experience, the Mojawa Run Plus, crafted by a team including former Apple engineers, offers stellar comfort and sound. Its 32-GB player and customizable EQ modes rival Shokz, though the touch controls can be finicky in water. And then there’s Suunto’s Sonic, a surprise entry from a fitness watch brand. It’s not flashy, but its wind-canceling microphones make calls clear even in 15 km/h gusts, and the lightweight design is perfect for hours of running. Bone conduction headphones aren’t just for athletes, though. They’re ideal for anyone who wants to stay aware of their surroundings—whether you’re biking in traffic, walking the dog, or just need to hear when someone’s at the door. The technology has matured, and these picks prove that you don’t have to sacrifice sound quality for safety.
why_it_matters: Understanding how audio technology works empowers you to choose devices that keep you safe and engaged in your environment, whether you're studying in a noisy café or biking to school.

The usual way we hear sound—through air vibrating against the eardrum—in this case, a small speaker that works alongside bone conduction.
An even more rugged waterproof rating that can withstand high-pressure, high-temperature water jets, not just submersion.
Buttons or surfaces on a device that respond to a finger tap or swipe, often used to adjust volume or skip tracks.
Microphone technology that uses algorithms to filter out the sound of rushing air, making phone calls clearer outdoors.

background_read: Bone conduction technology was originally developed for hearing aids and military communication, using transducers against the skull to bypass the eardrum. The brand Shokz (formerly AfterShokz) pioneered consumer bone conduction headphones in the early 2010s, making the category popular among runners and cyclists. Water and dust resistance are rated by IP codes—IP68 means completely dust-tight and waterproof beyond 1 meter, while IP69 can withstand high-pressure, high-temperature water jets. The shift to USB-C charging, now a common standard required by law for many devices in the European Union, finally reached Shokz's flagship model after years of proprietary cables. Wind-canceling microphones, like those in the Suunto Sonic (from the Finnish company best known for sports watches), use digital signal processing to filter out gusts that would ruin a phone call.

perspectives.description: Bone conduction headphones allow joggers and cyclists to hear traffic and pedestrians, reducing accidents. They also let people with certain hearing impairments enjoy music without blocking the ear canal.
Audiophiles argue that sound quality, especially deep bass, still lags behind traditional in-ear or over-ear headphones. Premium models can be cost-prohibitive for some teenagers.

The technology has matured from a buzzy novelty to a reliable product category, with major brands investing heavily in research and development. Regulatory moves toward common charger standards are pushing USB‑C adoption industry-wide.

Future versions might integrate heart-rate sensors, voice assistants, and even real-time language translation. As cities become denser, open-ear designs could become the default for safe mobile audio.
